title: Navigating the New Era: Dissecting India's Comprehensive Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026

# Navigating the New Era: Dissecting India's Comprehensive Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026

As seasoned professionals in the Indian tax and legal landscape, we're accustomed to its dynamic nature. Just when we've wrapped our heads around one set of changes, another significant piece of legislation arrives, reshaping the playing field. The latest entrant, the **Comprehensive Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026**, which received Presidential assent on **August 17, 2026**, is precisely that kind of landmark development. This Act isn't just a minor tweak; it's a strategic legislative exercise designed to foster economic growth, streamline compliance, and enhance India's global competitiveness.

This Act primarily amends three crucial pieces of legislation: the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, the **Income-tax Act, 2025**, and the **Finance Act, 2026**. It also formally repeals the Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, incorporating its provisions and introducing further refinements. While many provisions are deemed to have come into force from April 1, 2026, certain sections have specific effective dates. Let's dive deep into what this means for businesses and professionals alike.

## The Broader Vision: A Strategic Push for Growth and Certainty

What's the *big picture* behind this comprehensive amendment? The government's intent is quite clear: attract more foreign capital, give a boost to domestic electronics manufacturing, and provide much-needed "process certainty" for foreign cloud companies eyeing Indian data centres. Essentially, it's about making India an even more attractive destination for investment and business, while also adapting to the evolving digital and global economic landscape.

## Key Amendments – A Deep Dive

Let's break down the most impactful changes brought about by this new Act.

### 1. Payment Systems: Decoding the MDR Framework for Digital Transactions

One significant amendment impacts the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. Digital payments, especially UPI and RuPay, have become the backbone of our economy. But the framework around charges like Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) needed some flexibility.

**Old Provision (Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007)**
Previously, Section 10A referred to "electronic modes of payment prescribed under section 269SU of the Income-tax Act, 1961" (now Section 187 of Income Tax Act 2025) for determining which transactions were free of charges. This created a direct linkage that, at times, could be restrictive.

**New Provision (Amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007)**
The Act now empowers the Central Government to specify, by notification, "one or more electronic modes of payment" on which charges cannot be imposed. This delinks the provision from a specific section of the Income-tax Act, 2025, providing greater administrative flexibility. This amendment is effective from August 17, 2026.

| Feature           | Old Provision (Pre-Amendment)                                    | New Provision (Post-Amendment)                                                              |
| :---------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Reference for** | Linked to electronic payment modes prescribed under Section      | Central Government empowered to specify electronic modes by **notification**. |
| **zero-MDR**      | 269SU of ITA, 1961 (now Section 187 of ITA, 2025). |                                                                                             |
| **Implication**   | Less flexibility, direct statutory linkage.                      | Greater government flexibility to modify or introduce the zero-MDR framework. |

**Our Take:** This is a sensible move. It gives the government the agility to adapt to evolving payment technologies and policy needs without needing a legislative amendment every time. While Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has indicated that UPI payments will remain free for consumers, any future MDR will likely apply only to specific categories of merchant transactions. Businesses, particularly those accepting digital payments, should keep an eye out for forthcoming notifications from the government on this front. *Thoda detail mein, yeh flexibility kaafi kaam aayegi*.

### 2. Income Tax: Reshaping the Landscape for Foreign Investment Funds and Fund Managers

India has been actively trying to position itself as a global financial hub. A critical piece of this puzzle is making it easier for foreign investment funds to operate and manage their funds from India without triggering adverse tax consequences. The new Act significantly rationalises the "safe harbour" provisions under the Income-tax Act, 2025.

**Old Provision (Schedule I of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Safe Harbour for Eligible Investment Funds)**
Previously, foreign investment funds managing their activities from India had to adhere to a stringent set of conditions (around 13 conditions) to ensure that their activities would not constitute a "business connection" in India, thereby avoiding tax on their global income in India.

**New Provision (Amended Schedule I of the Income-tax Act, 2025)**
The Act introduces a revised Schedule I, simplifying the framework considerably by reducing the compliance conditions to just five core safeguards. The aim is to promote fund management activity within India. Key aspects include:
*   **Simplified Conditions:** Fewer hurdles for foreign funds to qualify for the safe harbour.
*   **Fund Manager Eligibility:** Conditions for eligible fund managers include registration under SEBI regulations and restrictions on their profit-sharing from the fund (generally not more than 20% for the manager and connected persons).
*   **Indian Participation:** The existing 5% limit on Indian participation in the fund corpus remains, with a ₹25 crore manager-contribution exclusion for the first three years.
*   **Compliance:** Eligible funds must furnish prescribed information to the income-tax authorities within 90 days from the end of the tax year.

| Feature                       | Old Provision (Pre-Amendment)                                       | New Provision (Post-Amendment)                                                          |
| :---------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------ | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Number of Conditions**      | Approximately 13 stringent conditions.                   | Reduced to 5 core conditions.                                                |
| **Objective**                 | Preventing business connection for offshore funds.                  | Simplifying for fund managers to relocate to India, providing tax certainty. |
| **Effective Date**            | As per ITA, 2025.                                                   | Effective from April 1, 2026.                                                |
| **Indian Participation Limit**| Generally 5% of corpus.                                             | Continues at 5%, with ₹25 crore exclusion for manager contribution initially. |

**Our Take:** This is *bada relief* for foreign investment funds looking at India. The rationalisation of conditions provides more clarity and reduces the compliance burden, potentially attracting more global capital and fund management talent to our shores. It’s a clear signal that India is open for financial business.

### 3. Boosting 'Make in India': Extended Tax Incentives for Electronics Manufacturing

The 'Make in India' initiative gets another strong push through amendments providing extended tax exemptions for electronics manufacturing and related activities.

**Old Provision (Schedule IV of the Income-tax Act, 2025 - Exemption for Electronics Manufacturing)**
Certain tax exemptions were available to foreign companies supplying capital goods, equipment, or tooling to Indian contract manufacturers of specified electronic goods. This exemption was generally available until the tax year 2030-31.

**New Provision (Amended Schedule IV of the Income-tax Act, 2025)**
The Act extends this crucial tax exemption for foreign companies engaging in contract manufacturing of specified electronic goods in India by another **ten years, i.e., until the tax year 2040-41**. This provides long-term policy certainty and encourages significant investments in the sector.
*   **Definition of 'Specified Electronic Goods':** The Act now clarifies and inserts a definition for "specified electronic goods", including items like mobile phones, laptops, servers, and their sub-assemblies.
*   **Rough Diamonds and Bonded Warehouses:** Similar exemptions are introduced for income derived by foreign companies from the sale of rough diamonds in notified special zones, and for income from storing components in bonded warehouses in India for supply to contract manufacturers of specified electronic goods. These exemptions are also available until March 31, 2041, with applicability from October 1, 2026, for these specific provisions.

| Feature                         | Old Provision (Pre-Amendment)                                       | New Provision (Post-Amendment)                                                      |
| :------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Exemption Period for**        | Until tax year 2030-31.                              | Extended until **tax year 2040-41**.                           |
| **Electronics Manufacturing**   |                                                                     |                                                                                     |
| **Definition of Specified**     | Not explicitly defined within the exemption provision.              | A clear definition of "specified electronic goods" has been inserted.|
| **Electronic Goods**            |                                                                     |                                                                                     |
| **Additional Exemptions**       | Limited scope.                                                      | Includes income from rough diamonds and bonded warehouse storage of components.|

**Our Take:** This extension is a strategic masterstroke. It signals India's long-term commitment to becoming a global electronics manufacturing hub. Foreign companies can now plan their investments with greater confidence, knowing the tax benefits are secure for a longer horizon. *Yeh toh ekdum clear policy certainty hai.*

### 4. Capital Markets: Tax Relief for FIIs in Government Securities

To deepen the Government Securities (G-Secs) market and encourage greater Foreign Institutional Investor (FII) participation, the Act introduces a significant tax exemption.

**Old Provision (Pre-Ordinance/Amendment)**
Before the Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026, FIIs and similar entities were typically subject to income tax on interest earned and capital gains arising from investments in G-Secs (e.g., interest at 20%, short-term capital gains at 30%, long-term at 12.5%).

**New Provision (Amendment to Income-tax Act, 2025)**
The Act now explicitly exempts Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) from paying income tax on:
*   Interest income earned from investments in Government Securities.
*   Capital gains arising from the sale, exchange, or transfer of such securities.
This exemption applies to income arising on or after April 1, 2026.

| Feature                                | Old Provision (Pre-Amendment)                   | New Provision (Post-Amendment)                                       |
| :------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Tax on Interest/Capital Gains for**  | Taxed as per applicable rates.       | **Exempt from income tax.**                           |
| **FIIs/BIS in G-Secs**                 |                                                 |                                                                      |
| **Effective Date**                     | -                                               | Applicable on income arising on or after April 1, 2026. |

**Our Take:** This is a fantastic step towards making Indian G-Secs more attractive to foreign investors. Lowering the tax barrier directly boosts returns for FIIs, which in turn helps in better financing government deficits and strengthens our capital markets.

### 5. Digital Infrastructure: Streamlining Data Centre Operations

Recognizing the critical role of data centres in the digital economy, the Act aims to facilitate easier operations for foreign cloud companies and promote investment in this sector.

**Key Changes:**
*   **Leased Ownership for Indian Companies:** For Indian companies operating specified data centres, the Act now explicitly allows a **leased model of ownership**, which was previously unclear or restricted.
*   **Removal of Notification Conditions:** The earlier requirement for notification of the foreign company or the specified data centre by the Central Government (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology) has been omitted, simplifying the setup process.
*   **Prescribed Conditions:** While notifications are removed, the specified data centres will still need to fulfil such conditions as may be prescribed by rules.

**Our Take:** This is a pragmatic amendment. By allowing leased models and removing bureaucratic hurdles of government notifications, India is making it much simpler and faster for both foreign and domestic players to set up and operate data centres. This is crucial for our digital economy's growth and attracting cloud service providers. *Compliance toh rahegi, but process easy ho gaya hai.*

### 6. Business Trusts: Streamlining Dividend Taxation

The Act also streamlines the taxation of dividend distributions by business trusts. It grants a uniform exemption to unitholders, irrespective of the tax regime adopted by the underlying Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV). However, SPVs opting for a concessional tax regime will face a higher surcharge of 25%. This aims to provide consistency while balancing revenue implications.

## Final Thoughts

The **Comprehensive Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026**, coming right after the introduction of the new Income-tax Act, 2025, underscores the government's proactive approach to legislative reform. The changes are largely aimed at promoting investment, simplifying certain compliance aspects, and providing tax certainty in key growth sectors. Whether it's the recalibration of digital payment regulations, the encouragement for foreign funds and electronics manufacturers, or the boost for G-Secs, each amendment reflects a strategic intent to strengthen India's economic fabric.

As CAs and legal analysts, our role is to meticulously understand these nuances. The varied effective dates for different provisions mean careful navigation is required. Staying updated isn't just a choice; it's a professional imperative to advise our clients effectively. *Toh, ab is naye Act ko ekdum achhe se samajhna padega, kya bolte ho?*
